sections.heading: An ambush predator
sections.pro:
A musky does not hunt by running down prey across open water. It holds in or beside cover and strikes from short range. It sees well in low light and has a lateral line that reads vibration and pressure from several feet away. That is why blades thump, why rattles and prop baits make noise, and why a lure that changes direction at the boat gets hit: the fish tracks the vibration first and commits on the change.

The strike zone runs all the way to the boat. A fish that followed the lure for forty feet is still deciding at the rod tip. The figure-8 is not a flourish. It is the last and best chance on every cast.
sections.yourJob: Keep the lure moving to the boat every cast. The strike zone includes the last ten feet.

sections.heading: Temperature runs the metabolism
sections.pro:
A musky is cold-blooded. Its feeding speed tracks the water temperature. In warm water the fish is fast, the strike window is short, and fast lures draw reaction strikes. In cold water the fish is slow, the strike window is long, and big slow lures that stay in front of it win. The number on the fish finder decides lure speed before anything else does.

Above the high 70s the fish are stressed. A long fight and a slow release in that water can kill a fish that swam away looking fine. In October on this chain that is not the problem; cold is. But the rule is the same: read the temperature at launch and plan around it.
sections.yourJob: Read the water temperature off the fish finder at launch and tell him.

sections.heading: Why follows happen
sections.pro:
A follow is a fish that committed to the lure and then lost interest. It saw something worth chasing and did not get the trigger it wanted. Three causes cover most follows: the speed was wrong, the size was wrong, or the lure never changed direction. Speed is the most common. A lazy follow in cold water usually wants slower; a hot follow that turns away at the boat usually wants a faster, wider turn.

Follows are information, not failure. They tell you fish are on the spot and the presentation is close. The figure-8 turns a share of them into hits. The log turns the rest into a pattern.
sections.yourJob: Watch behind his lure on every retrieve. Say 'fish' the moment you see one.

sections.heading: Fifteen lakes, one system
sections.pro:
The Cisco Chain is fifteen named lakes: Cisco (506 to 567 acres by source, 20 ft), Thousand Island (1,078 acres, 81 ft), Big (771 acres), West Bay (368 acres), East Bay (277 acres), Mamie (337 to 400 acres by source, 10 ft), Indian (129 acres), Poor (106 acres), Fishhawk (77 acres, 8 ft), Lindsley (156 acres, 46 ft), Clearwater (172 acres, 10 ft), Big African (86 acres), Little African (31 acres), Record (68 acres, 16 ft), and Morley (59 acres). Together they hold about 4,000 acres of water and 270 miles of shoreline.

Most of the chain is in Gogebic County, Michigan. Big, West Bay, and Mamie cross the line into Vilas County, Wisconsin, which makes them boundary water with their own rulebook.

The lakes were not connected by navigable water originally. Logging operations in the 1800s changed that, and a dam built in 1931 raised the water four to five feet and created the channels boats use today. Clearwater is the exception: no navigable channel, only a small creek a few hundred yards to Little African. Water levels vary only about six inches through the year, so the structure you learn stays where it is.
sections.yourJob: Learn the names. He will say 'Lindsley' and you need to know it is the deep one.

sections.heading: Two deep basins, many bowls
sections.pro:
Thousand Island is the chain's deep basin. The Michigan DNR survey put it at 81 ft maximum, with a thermocline between 17 and 26 ft in midsummer and no oxygen below 50 ft in summer. Visibility is 12 ft by Secchi disk. The shoals are steep and made of sand, gravel, and fibrous peat. Weeds are abundant, mostly submergent and floating species, and the lake has logs and sunken islands for cover. Lindsley is the second basin at 46 ft.

Everything else is mostly under 20 ft: Cisco at 20, Record at 16, Mamie at 10, Clearwater at 10, Fishhawk at 8. These are bowls. They have weeds across most of the bottom and little deep edge.

The two kinds of lake fish differently in fall. A deep lake stratifies in summer and turns over when the surface cools to the temperature of the deep water, usually in October. For about a week it is murky and slow. A bowl never stratified, so it never turns over. It warms and cools with the air and fishes as one big weed flat until the weeds die.
sections.yourJob: When the plan says a lake is a bowl, expect weeds everywhere and no deep edge.

sections.heading: What the musky eat here
sections.pro:
The DNR species list for Thousand Island includes cisco, yellow perch, bluegill, rock bass, white sucker, walleye, northern pike, smallmouth bass, and black crappie. Three of those matter most to a musky angler. Cisco are pelagic: they live in open water over the basin in summer, below the thermocline, and spawn on gravel and rock in late fall. Perch and bluegill live in the weeds. Suckers are everywhere and are the bait shop's fall offering.

Lure size and depth follow the forage. Over the basin in cold water, a big cisco-shaped crank or rubber bait at 10 to 20 ft imitates the main course. On the weed flats, perch colors and perch sizes make sense. A 14-inch sucker under a float is not an imitation; it is the real thing.
sections.yourJob: Tell him what the sonar shows: a cloud at 20 ft over the basin is cisco; dots in the weeds are perch.

sections.heading: Musky status, lake by lake
sections.pro:
Wisconsin's DNR rates its musky waters by angling quality and reproduction. Big Lake, Mamie Lake, and West Bay Lake are all Class A1, Category 1. A1 means trophy water: the fish are relatively few, but the ones you meet are large. Category 1 means the population sustains itself by natural reproduction with no stocking.

On the Michigan side, Thousand Island has been stocked with northern-strain muskellunge, and the chain has seen tiger musky and lake trout plants over the years. The 1993 DNR report notes two large musky seen in the 1988 survey, one about 25 pounds, and no natural reproduction documented in that lake. Michigan's state record northern muskellunge, 49.75 pounds, came from Thousand Island in 1980.

Put those facts together and the approach is clear. This is low-density, big-fish water. Fewer spots, more time on each, and a follow is a real result. Log every one.
sections.yourJob: A1 means the fish are few and big. A follow here is a win. Log it.

sections.heading: Access
sections.pro:
There are four public landings on the chain. Thousand Island has a state-maintained access on the east shore: a wide concrete ramp, a loading dock, vault toilets, and deep water right at the ramp, so any trailered boat launches easily. Cisco Lake has a public landing. Big Lake has a landing and a marina on its south end with rentals and supplies. Mamie Lake has a gravel launch at the Spring Creek inlet, about a mile and a half from Angler's Isle.

Every lake on the chain is reachable by water through the channels, so on a calm day any dock on the chain is a launch. On a windy day the closest landing to the lake in the plan saves a long run.
sections.yourJob: Know which landing is closest to the lake in the plan.

sections.heading: Spring, ice-out to 60°F
sections.pro: Musky spawn soon after ice-out in shallow bays, and for a few weeks after that they are thin, tired, and shallow. Warming bays with dark bottoms and new weed growth hold them. Smaller lures than you would throw in fall, worked slowly, draw the strikes. This chapter is an outline for version one. Fill it from the log after the first spring on the chain, when you know which bays warm first and which weeds come up first.
sections.yourJob: Spring is for next year. Read this in April.

sections.heading: Summer, 60 to 78°F
sections.pro: In summer the weeds are at full height and the outside weed edge is the line to fish. On Thousand Island some fish suspend over the basin near the thermocline, 17 to 26 ft down, following cisco. Dawn, dusk, and night fish best; midday fish are tucked in the thickest cover. Fast lures work because the fish are fast: bucktails burned over the weeds, topwater at night. This is an outline for version one. The summer notes will come from the log.
sections.yourJob: Summer notes go here after the first season.

sections.heading: Early fall, 72 down to 60°F
sections.pro:
This is where the chain was on September 24, 2026. Bill's report from All Northwoods put the water at 63 to 71°F, the musky bite picking up after three slow weeks, fish on the shallow weed flats, and topwater baits the most effective lure early and late in the day. The weeds are still green and standing. Perch are on the flats, and the musky are with them.

The fish are still fast. Topwater walked over the flats at first light and at dusk, bucktails run fast through the same water in between, and a spinnerbait when the wind comes up. Low light is everything in this stretch: the flats are shallow, the water is clear, and a fish on a flat at noon under a bright sun is a rare thing.

The bait shop started stocking musky suckers in the first half of September. By the September 24 report anglers were trying them, with no verdict yet on whether they beat artificial baits at those temperatures. At 63 to 71°F the artificial bite is usually better and the suckers die fast. Keep the suckers for later.
sections.yourJob: Dawn and dusk are not optional in early fall. Be on the water before the sun.

sections.heading: Fall transition, 60 down to 52°F
sections.pro:
As the water drops through the 50s the flats change. Shallow weeds brown off and lie down, and the perch leave them. The musky slide out to the outside weed edge, to the points, to the inside turns where the edge pockets in, and to the first break into deeper water. On the bowls this means the last green weeds, wherever they are. On Thousand Island it means the steep shoals and the edges of the sunken islands.

Slow down. The fish will still eat, but they will not chase. Gliders worked with long pauses, jerkbaits that dive and rise, and minnow cranks twitched along the edge replace the burned bucktail. Follows increase before hits do, and most of the follows are a speed problem: the fish wants it slower and wants a pause.

The daily clock changes too. Dawn matters less because the water is coldest then. The warmest hours of the afternoon and the hour into dusk matter more. On a sunny day after a cold night, a bowl like Fishhawk or Mamie can warm two or three degrees by mid-afternoon and turn on.
sections.yourJob: Watch the weeds. Green and standing means stay. Brown and flat means move to the edge.

sections.heading: Turnover
sections.pro:
A deep lake stratifies in summer: warm water on top, cold water below, a thermocline between. On Thousand Island the DNR measured that thermocline between 17 and 26 ft in midsummer, with no oxygen below 50 ft. When the surface cools to the temperature of the deep water, usually somewhere around 50 to 55°F in October, the layers mix. That is turnover. The water goes murky with debris lifted off the bottom, it can smell of bottom, and the fishing drops for about a week while the lake settles.

Lindsley, at 46 ft, turns over too. The bowls do not. Fishhawk, Mamie, Clearwater, and the other shallow lakes never stratified, so there is nothing to mix. They keep fishing while the deep lakes recover.

The move is to move. If Thousand Island looks brown and bubbly, run to a bowl or to a neck between lakes, where current keeps the water clean. The exact timing is reasoning, not a measured fact for this chain; the log will give the date after a season or two.
sections.yourJob: Look at the water and smell it. Murky, bubbles, bottom smell: turnover. Say it.

sections.heading: Late fall, under 52°F
sections.pro:
This is the season for the biggest fish of the year. The water is cold, the fish are slow, and they are feeding up for winter on the largest prey they can find. Three presentations cover it. Live suckers, 12 to 16 inches, fished under a float or dragged slowly off a break on a quick-strike rig. Big soft plastics, counted down to the depth the fish are holding and pulled slowly. Deep crankbaits trolled along the breaks and over the basin where the sonar shows bait.

The quick-strike rig is what makes sucker fishing a release fishery. You set the hook when the fish takes, not after a long wait, so the hooks are in the jaw and not in the throat.

The clock inverts from summer. The warmest hours of the afternoon beat dawn. Dusk still matters. On this chain the boundary water season on Big, Mamie, and West Bay closes December 31, while the Michigan-only lakes stay open to possession through March 15 and to catch-and-release all year, so late fall and ice-up are the end of the harvest window on the boundary lakes only.
sections.yourJob: Dress for cold. A float that moves is the only thing you need to watch.

sections.heading: Cisco spawn, late November
sections.pro:
Thousand Island holds cisco. Cisco spawn in late fall, in the last part of November, on gravel and rock shoals, at dusk and after dark, and the spawn clusters around the full moon. In 2026 the November full moon is the 24th. When the cisco come up onto the shoals, the biggest musky in the lake follow them, and for a few nights the hardest-bottom shoals near deep water hold the fish of the year.

Fish it with the biggest rubber baits and the biggest cranks over hard bottom at dusk and into the dark, and drop a sucker off the edge of the shoal. The night catch peak in the lunar data is at the full moon, which lines up with the spawn. Find the gravel on the sonar before the light goes, mark it, and come back to it in the dark.
sections.yourJob: Find the hard bottom on the sonar before dark. Lights and gloves ready.

sections.heading: Dawn and dusk
sections.pro: Low light is the strongest daily factor in musky fishing. The hour either side of sunrise and the hour either side of sunset are the windows. Fish that sit in cover at noon move onto the flats and the edges when the light drops. In clear water like Thousand Island's 12 ft of visibility, low light also hides the boat and the line. The plan computes sunrise and sunset for the chain each day and lists both windows.
sections.yourJob: Be on the first spot before the window opens, not during it.

sections.heading: The moon, with the numbers
sections.pro:
Musky anglers have argued about the moon for a century. The data settles some of it. A 2014 study in PLOS ONE analyzed 341,959 musky catch records from Muskies Inc. logs from 1970 to 2013. Catch rose around both the full moon and the new moon. The maximum effect was about 5 percent: an angler who fished only on peak lunar days would catch about 5 percent more fish than one who fished random days. The effect was stronger for fish over 102 cm, about 40 inches. At night, the peak was at the full moon, not the new moon.

Dettloff's records from the Chippewa Flowage, a trophy water, put 34.7 percent of fish over 40 inches in the full moon period, against the 25 percent you would expect if the moon did nothing.

Within a day, anglers use four events: moon overhead and moon underfoot are the majors, moonrise and moonset the minors. The published studies do not test those four directly, so treat them as angler consensus. The honest conclusion is this: the moon decides when to be on your best spot, not whether to go. The plan lists the windows and tells you when one stacks on dusk.
sections.yourJob: The plan lists the windows. Keep the clock and call them.

sections.heading: Pressure
sections.pro:
Barometric pressure falling ahead of a front is the classic feeding trigger. The wind builds, the sky thickens from the west, the pressure drops, and fish that were tucked in cover come out and eat. The day or two after the front passes is the opposite: high pressure, clear sky, often a north wind, and fish that hold tight and will not chase.

The app pulls hourly pressure from Open-Meteo, computes the change over the last three hours, and shows it in inches of mercury with a word: falling, steady, or rising. A fall of about 0.03 inHg or more in three hours counts as falling. It also looks back through the last two days for the pressure minimum that marks a front and tells the planner how many hours ago it passed.
sections.yourJob: Read the trend arrow in the plan before launch and tell him.

sections.heading: Wind
sections.pro:
Wind moves the top layer of water, and with it plankton. Baitfish follow the plankton, and musky follow the bait. The shoreline the wind blows against, the windward side, collects all three. On this chain that means the points and flats facing the wind fish best, and the calm lee side fishes worst. Wind also breaks up the surface and the light, which lets fish feed shallower in daylight. Spinnerbaits and bucktails fish well in chop; topwater does not once the waves build past a foot.

The spot list in the plan already weights spots by the wind direction you entered, so the top of the list is the windward structure.
sections.yourJob: Keep the boat upwind so he casts with the wind across the spot.

sections.heading: Sky and fronts
sections.pro: Cloud cover extends low light into the middle of the day. An overcast sky with a chop can make noon fish like dusk, and the flats and edges stay worth fishing straight through. A bluebird sky after a front does the reverse. The fish are there, but they sit in the thickest cover and the inside turns, and the best you often get is a follow that will not commit. On those days slow down, go smaller, fish the moon windows, and log every follow. The pattern shows up in the log before it shows up in the net.
sections.yourJob: On a bluebird day expect follows. Log them all.

sections.heading: The vocabulary
sections.pro: A weed flat is a broad shallow area of weed growth, 3 to 10 ft, that fish roam in low light. A weed edge is where the weeds stop against deeper water; the outside edge is the ambush line most of the year, the inside edge the line between the weeds and the shore. A point reaches into deep water. An inside turn is a pocket in the breakline where bait collects. A saddle is a shallow ridge between two deeper areas. A hump is a sunken island. A break is a sharp depth change. A neck is a channel between two lakes. An inlet is where water enters, an outlet where it leaves. Rock, wood, island, and shoal mean what they say, and on this chain the shoals are steep and made of sand, gravel, and peat. The app's spot types use exactly these words.
sections.yourJob: Point at the structure on the map and say its name. That is the job.

sections.heading: Weeds
sections.pro: Not all weeds are equal. Cabbage, the broadleaf pondweed, is the musky weed: it grows tall and open, a fish can move through it, and it holds perch. Coontail is dense and holds fish on its edge rather than inside it. Milfoil mats on the surface and is mostly a nuisance. Green weeds hold fish. Brown weeds that have died and lain down do not, and in fall the fish leave them for the last green growth and the edges. When a lure comes back with weed on it, look at what kind and whether it is green.
sections.yourJob: Lift a weed on the lure and name it. Green cabbage is good news.

sections.heading: Reading the DNR map
sections.pro: A depth contour map shows lines of equal depth. Where the lines run close together the bottom drops fast: a break. Where they spread apart the bottom is flat. A shallow flat with a steep edge is the classic musky spot, and on Thousand Island the DNR describes exactly that kind of shoal: steep, sand and gravel and peat, with abundant weeds on top. Necks and inlet mouths are marked where the shoreline pinches. Islands have a shallow side, where the contours spread, and a steep side, where they bunch. The app shows each lake's map where one is on file. Find the steepest break near the launch and start there.
sections.yourJob: Open the lake map in the app and find the steepest break near the launch.

sections.heading: The families
sections.pro: Bucktails are inline spinners, fast search baits for warm water, 60°F and up. Topwater baits walk or churn on the surface at dawn, dusk, and on calm overcast days from about 58°F up, as the September 24 report confirmed on this chain. Gliders move side to side on rod pulls with pauses and are the first choice from 45 to 65°F. Jerkbaits dive and rise; the rise is the trigger, and they fish the same band. Crankbaits run 4 to 8 ft twitched or 8 to 20 ft trolled, 40 to 70°F. Rubber baits, the big soft plastics, count down to any depth and fish slowest and coldest, 38 to 62°F. Spinnerbaits fish wind and dirty water through and over weeds. Live suckers on quick-strike rigs are the cold-water bait, under 58°F. The app's lure catalog carries the same bands and tells you when not to throw each one.
sections.yourJob: Tie on the next lure before he asks for it.

sections.heading: Speed is the first variable
sections.pro: Most follows that do not turn into hits are a speed problem, not a lure problem. Warm water wants faster. Cold water wants slower, with pauses. Before you change the lure, change the speed. A fish that follows lazily and sinks away is asking for slower and a pause. A fish that follows hot, right on the lure, and turns off at the boat is asking for a faster, wider figure-8. Only after speed has been tried both ways does size change, and only after that does the lure family change.
sections.yourJob: Count his cadence. If follows stay lazy, suggest slower; if they turn away hot, suggest faster.

sections.heading: The figure-8
sections.pro: Every cast ends in a figure-8 at the boat. Rod tip deep in the water, wide turns, and the lure speeds up on the turns. A following fish that has tracked the lure forty feet is still deciding, and the direction change is the trigger it was waiting for. Most boat-side hits come on the second turn, when the fish has committed to the new direction. A short, lazy L at the boat wastes the follow. The 8 is where the follow becomes the fish.
sections.yourJob: Watch the 8 with the net in hand. Stay back from the rod.

sections.heading: Boat control
sections.pro: Position the boat upwind of the structure so the casts go across it with the wind, not along it and not against it. Keep the boat off the structure, not on it, especially in water with 12 ft of visibility where a fish on a shallow flat can see the hull. Run the trolling motor steady and quiet; starts and stops spook more fish than steady movement. On a drift, set the drift to carry the boat along the edge so every cast lands on the line that matters.
sections.yourJob: You run the trolling motor. Keep the boat where he can cast across the edge.

sections.heading: Trolling and suckers
sections.pro:
Trolling covers deep water that casting cannot reach. Run 2.5 to 4 mph along breaks and over the basin where the sonar shows bait. Line out sets the running depth. Rods go in holders and the rod tips are the instruments: a steady throb means the lure is clean, a dead tip means it picked up weeds. Michigan allows trolling on these lakes; on the boundary lakes each angler may run up to three lines.

Suckers go on quick-strike rigs, two hooks placed so you set on the strike, not after a wait. Never let a fish swallow a sucker. Set when the float moves off and keeps moving.
sections.yourJob: Rod tips and the float are your two jobs when we troll or soak suckers.

sections.heading: Rod, reel, line
sections.pro: A musky rod is long and heavy, 8 to 9 ft, with the backbone to move a 10-inch lure all day and set a hook through a hard jaw. The reel is a large casting reel with a strong drag. Line is 80 to 100 lb braid; it does not stretch, so the hookset reaches the fish. The leader is 100 lb or heavier fluorocarbon, or wire, 12 to 18 inches, because a musky's teeth cut anything lighter. Check the leader after every fish and every snag, and retie when you find a nick.
sections.yourJob: Check leaders for nicks after every fish and every snag.

sections.heading: Release tools and fish care
sections.pro: The tools come out before the first cast: a big net with a deep bag, a bump board for measuring, hook cutters, long-nosed pliers, and jaw spreaders. The fish stays in the water in the net while the hooks come out. Cut a hook rather than tear it. Then measure in the boat on the board, tip of the lower jaw to the tip of the tail, which is how Muskies Inc. defines length. Girth, if you want a weight, goes around the widest point of the body; the common estimate is length times girth times girth divided by 800. One quick photo and the fish goes back. The whole handling should take less time than reading this paragraph.
sections.yourJob: Lay the tools out on the deck before the first cast. Net, cutters, pliers, board.

sections.heading: Three size limits on one chain
sections.pro:
Two rulebooks apply on the Cisco Chain, and a fish that is legal on one lake is not legal a channel away. On the Michigan-only lakes the statewide inland rule applies: 42 inches minimum, one muskellunge per angler per license year, registration within 24 hours of harvest online, in the DNR app, or by phone, and a possession season from the first Saturday in June through March 15. Catch-and-immediate-release is open all year.

Big, Mamie, and West Bay are Michigan-Wisconsin boundary waters. There the minimum is 50 inches, the possession season runs from the first Saturday in June through December 31, registration is mandatory, a valid license from either state is good, you follow the rules of the state whose water you are in, and each angler may run up to three lines.

Some websites show a 46-inch figure for Michigan musky. That is the Master Angler award entry minimum, not a regulation. It is never the rule on any lake here.
sections.yourJob: Know which lake you are on. The rule changes when you cross a neck into Big.

sections.heading: Pike and licenses
sections.pro: You will catch northern pike while musky fishing on this chain. Pike size rules vary by lake and the Michigan-only chain lakes appear in a county list in the 2026 digest with a special pike rule, so check the current rule for the lake you are on before keeping one. Carry the right license: Michigan for the Michigan-only lakes, and either state's license on Big, Mamie, and West Bay. Fish inside the state your license matches when you can, and know where the line runs on those three lakes.
sections.yourJob: Carry both licenses if you fish Big, Mamie, or West Bay.

sections.heading: Before launch
sections.pro: A good first mate makes the boat ready before the angler steps in. The tools are laid out on the deck: net rigged and open, cutters, pliers, board, spreaders. The lures the plan recommends are tied on or in the top of the box. The plan is read aloud: the top window and when it opens, the top spot and why, the lures and the speed, and the rule for this lake. Then the water temperature is read off the fish finder at the dock and compared to the number in the plan. If it moved more than two degrees, say so, because the plan may change.
sections.yourJob: Read him the plan's top window and top spot before you leave the dock.

sections.heading: On the water
sections.pro: You run the trolling motor and keep the boat where the casts cross the structure. You call the depth under the boat and when it changes fast. You call the weeds: green or brown, cabbage or coontail, when they start and when they stop on the sonar. You watch behind his lure on every retrieve and say 'fish' the moment you see a shape. You keep the clock and say when a window opens and when it closes. And you log every follow before the next cast, with the lure, the speed, and how the fish acted, because the log is where the pattern lives.
sections.yourJob: Say what you see. Fish, weeds, depth, bait. Short words.

sections.heading: When a fish is on
sections.pro: The net goes in the water first, not last. Lead the fish head-first into the bag; a musky netted tail-first thrashes out. Once it is in the net, the net stays in the water with the fish in it until the tools are in hand. Cutters come first for any hook that is deep or awkward. Then the board, measured the Muskies Inc. way, lower jaw tip to tail tip. Then one photo. Then the release, holding the fish upright in the water until it kicks away on its own. Say the order out loud if you need to. Net, cutters, board, photo, release.
sections.yourJob: Net, then cutters, then board, then photo, then release. In that order.

sections.heading: Nothing is happening
sections.pro:
When an hour has gone by with no follow, run the checklist in order, and change one thing at a time. This is reasoning, not sourced.

First, the clock. Are you inside a light window or a moon window, or between them? If between, nothing may be wrong except the hour. Second, the weeds. Lift one on the lure: green and standing means the flat is alive; brown and lying down means the fish have moved to the edge. Third, position. Are the casts landing on the edge of the structure or on top of it? Fish on the edge do not see a lure on top. Fourth, speed. The wrong speed costs more follows than the wrong lure, so change it before you change anything else. Fifth, bait. Does the sonar show anything? No bait usually means no musky. Sixth, wind. Has it shifted off this structure onto another?

Give each change twenty minutes before you judge it. Two changes at once teach you nothing.
sections.yourJob: Keep the clock, call the weeds, say what the sonar shows.

sections.heading: A follow without a strike
sections.pro:
A follow tells you three things: the fish is there, the lure is close to right, and the trigger is missing. Respond in order, and give each step a few casts. This is reasoning, not sourced.

Speed first. Faster in warm water; slower, with pauses, under 55°F. Then the figure-8: wider turns, deeper rod tip, faster on the turns. Then size: up a size if the fish looked big and lazy, down a size if it looked nervous. Then a different lure family with the same action, a glider for a jerkbait, a prop bait for a walker. Then leave and come back in the next window, because a fish that followed once will often eat the second time if the light has changed.

Mark the spot and the time. A follow is a located fish, and a located fish in trophy water is the best information you will get all day.
sections.yourJob: Log the follow before the next cast. Net ready. Watch the fish on the 8 and say where it is.

sections.heading: When to adjust
sections.pro:
Four things can change, and each has a signal. This is reasoning, not sourced.

Depth. Change it when follows come up from well under the lure, when bait shows deeper on the sonar than the lure is running, or when the water has dropped under 55°F and the fish have left the flats. Count the lure down or move to a deeper-running family.

Retrieve. Lazy follows mean change the speed or add pauses. Hot follows that turn away at the boat mean a bigger, faster figure-8.

Boat position. Change it when the wind has shifted, when the casts are going with the wind down the structure instead of across it, or when the boat is sitting on top of a shallow spot in water with 12 ft of visibility.

Location. Leave when two windows have passed with no sign of a fish, when the weeds on this spot are dead, when the sonar shows no bait, or when the wind now loads a different lake or a different point.

Every time Dad changes one of these, write a note in the trip: what changed, why in his words, and later, what happened. Over a season those notes become the chain's playbook.
sections.yourJob: Time the twenty minutes, say when a window opens or closes, next lure ready, and write down why he changed.
